L605: locals()【43†¶】
L606: 
L607: 
L608: Return a mapping object representing the current local symbol table, with variable names as the keys, and their currently bound references as the values.
L609: 
L610: At module scope, as well as when using 【23†`exec()`】 or 【22†`eval()`】 with a single namespace, this function returns the same namespace as 【30†`globals()`】.
L611: At class scope, it returns the namespace that will be passed to the metaclass constructor.
L612: 
L613: When using `exec()` or `eval()` with separate local and global arguments, it returns the local namespace passed in to the function call.
L614: In all of the above cases, each call to `locals()` in a given frame of execution will return the same mapping object. Changes made through the mapping object returned from `locals()` will be visible as assigned, reassigned, or deleted local variables, and assigning, reassigning, or deleting local variables will immediately affect the contents of the returned mapping object.
L615: In an 【202†optimized scope】 (including functions, generators, and coroutines), each call to `locals()` instead returns a fresh dictionary containing the current bindings of the function’s local variables and any nonlocal cell references.
L616: In this case, name binding changes made via the returned dict are not written back to the corresponding local variables or nonlocal cell references, and assigning, reassigning, or deleting local variables and nonlocal cell references does not affect the contents of previously returned dictionaries.
L617: Calling `locals()` as part of a comprehension in a function, generator, or coroutine is equivalent to calling it in the containing scope, except that the comprehension’s initialised iteration variables will be included. In other scopes, it behaves as if the comprehension were running as a nested function.
L618: 
L619: Calling `locals()` as part of a generator expression is equivalent to calling it in a nested generator function.
L620: Changed in version 3.12: The behaviour of `locals()` in a comprehension has been updated as described in 【203†PEP 709†peps.python.org】.

L667: This is the ultimate base class of all other classes. It has methods that are common to all instances of Python classes. When the constructor is called, it returns a new featureless object. The constructor does not accept any arguments.

L673: 
L674: 
L675: Convert an integer number to an octal string prefixed with “0o”. The result is a valid Python expression. If integer is not a Python 【37†`int`】 object, it has to define an 【81†`__index__()`】 method that returns an integer. For example:
L676: 
L677:     >>> oct(8)
L678:     '0o10'
L679:     >>> oct(-56)
L680:     '-0o70'
L681: If you want to convert an integer number to an octal string either with the prefix “0o” or not, you can use either of the following ways.
L682: 
L683:     >>> '%#o' % 10, '%o' % 10
L684:     ('0o12', '12')
L685:     >>> format(10, '#o'), format(10, 'o')
L686:     ('0o12', '12')
L687:     >>> f'{10:#o}', f'{10:o}'
L688:     ('0o12', '12')
L689:

L693: open(file, mode='r', buffering=-1, encoding=None, errors=None, newline=None, closefd=True, opener=None)【51†¶】
L694: Open file and return a corresponding 【208†file object】. If the file cannot be opened, an 【209†`OSError`】 is raised. See 【210†Reading and writing files】 for more examples of how to use this function.
L695: 
L696: file is a 【211†path-like object】 giving the pathname (absolute or relative to the current working directory) of the file to be opened or an integer file descriptor of the file to be wrapped. (If a file descriptor is given, it is closed when the returned I/O object is closed unless closefd is set to `False`.)
L697: mode is an optional string that specifies the mode in which the file is opened. It defaults to `'r'` which means open for reading in text mode. Other common values are `'w'` for writing (truncating the file if it already exists), `'x'` for exclusive creation, and `'a'` for appending (which on some Unix systems, means that all writes append to the end of the file regardless of the current seek position).
L698: In text mode, if encoding is not specified, UTF-8 is used by default; if 【212†Python UTF-8 Mode】 is disabled, 【213†`locale.getencoding()`】 is called to get the current locale encoding. (For reading and writing raw bytes use binary mode and leave encoding unspecified.) The available modes are:
L699: Character  | Meaning
L700: --- | ---
L701: `'r'`  | open for reading (default)
L702: `'w'`  | open for writing, truncating the file first
L703: `'x'`  | open for exclusive creation, failing if the file already exists
L704: `'a'`  | open for writing, appending to the end of file if it exists
L705: `'b'`  | binary mode
L706: `'t'`  | text mode (default)
L707: `'+'`  | open for updating (reading and writing)
L708: The default mode is `'r'` (open for reading text, a synonym of `'rt'`). Modes `'w+'` and `'w+b'` open and truncate the file. Modes `'r+'` and `'r+b'` open the file with no truncation.
L709: As mentioned in the 【214†Overview】, Python distinguishes between binary and text I/O. Files opened in binary mode (including `'b'` in the mode argument) return contents as 【94†`bytes`】 objects without any decoding. In text mode (the default, or when `'t'` is included in the mode argument), the contents of the file are returned as 【151†`str`】, the bytes having been first decoded using the default encoding or using the specified encoding if given.
L710: 
L711: Note
L712: Python doesn’t depend on the underlying operating system’s notion of text files; all the processing is done by Python itself, and is therefore platform-independent.
L713: buffering is an optional integer used to set the buffering policy. Pass 0 to switch buffering off (only allowed in binary mode), 1 to select line buffering (only usable when writing in text mode), and an integer > 1 to indicate the size in bytes of a fixed-size chunk buffer. Note that specifying a buffer size this way applies for binary buffered I/O, but `TextIOWrapper` (i.e., files opened with `mode='r+'`) would have another buffering.
L714: To disable buffering in `TextIOWrapper`, consider using the `write_through` flag for 【215†`io.TextIOWrapper.reconfigure()`】. When no buffering argument is given, the default buffering policy works as follows:
L715:   * Binary files are buffered in fixed-size chunks; the size of the buffer is `max(min(blocksize, 8 MiB), DEFAULT_BUFFER_SIZE)` when the device block size is available. On most systems, the buffer will typically be 128 kilobytes long.
L716: 
L717:   * “Interactive” text files (files for which 【216†`isatty()`】 returns `True`) use line buffering. Other text files use the policy described above for binary files.
L718: encoding is the name of the encoding used to decode or encode the file. This should only be used in text mode. The default encoding is UTF-8; if 【212†Python UTF-8 Mode】 is disabled, the default is platform-dependent (whatever 【213†`locale.getencoding()`】 returns). Any 【217†text encoding】 supported by Python can be used, and `encoding="locale"` specifies the current locale encoding explicitly. See the 【218†`codecs`】 module for the list of supported encodings.
L719: errors is an optional string that specifies how encoding and decoding errors are to be handled—this cannot be used in binary mode. A variety of standard error handlers are available, though any error handling name that has been registered with 【219†`codecs.register_error()`】 is also valid. The standard names can be found in 【220†Error Handlers】.
L720: 
L721: newline determines how to parse newline characters from the stream. It can be `None`, `''`, `'\n'`, `'\r'`, and `'\r\n'`. It works as follows:
L722:   * When reading input from the stream, if newline is `None`, universal newlines mode is enabled. Lines in the input can end in `'\n'`, `'\r'`, or `'\r\n'`, and these are translated into `'\n'` before being returned to the caller. If it is `''`, universal newlines mode is enabled, but line endings are returned to the caller untranslated. If it has any of the other legal values, input lines are only terminated by the given string, and the line ending is returned to the caller untranslated.
L723:   * When writing output to the stream, if newline is `None`, any `'\n'` characters written are translated to the system default line separator, 【221†`os.linesep`】. If newline is `''` or `'\n'`, no translation takes place. If newline is any of the other legal values, any `'\n'` characters written are translated to the given string.
L724: If closefd is `False` and a file descriptor rather than a filename was given, the underlying file descriptor will be kept open when the file is closed. If a filename is given closefd must be `True` (the default); otherwise, an error will be raised.
L725: A custom opener can be used by passing a callable as opener. The underlying file descriptor for the file object is then obtained by calling opener with (file, flags). opener must return an open file descriptor (passing 【222†`os.open`】 as opener results in functionality similar to passing `None`).
L726: 
L727: The newly created file is 【223†non-inheritable】.
L728: The following example uses the 【224†dir_fd】 parameter of the 【222†`os.open()`】 function to open a file relative to a given directory:
L729: 
L730:     >>> import os
L731:     >>> dir_fd = os.open('somedir', os.O_RDONLY)
L732:     >>> def opener(path, flags):
L733:     ...     return os.open(path, flags, dir_fd=dir_fd)
L734:     ...
L735:     >>> with open('spamspam.txt', 'w', opener=opener) as f:
L736:     ...     print('This will be written to somedir/spamspam.txt', file=f)
L737:     ...
L738:     >>> os.close(dir_fd)  # don't leak a file descriptor
L739: The type of 【208†file object】 returned by the `open()` function depends on the mode. When `open()` is used to open a file in a text mode (`'w'`, `'r'`, `'wt'`, `'rt'`, etc.), it returns a subclass of 【225†`io.TextIOBase`】 (specifically 【226†`io.TextIOWrapper`】). When used to open a file in a binary mode with buffering, the returned class is a subclass of 【227†`io.BufferedIOBase`】.
L740: The exact class varies: in read binary mode, it returns an 【228†`io.BufferedReader`】; in write binary and append binary modes, it returns an 【229†`io.BufferedWriter`】, and in read/write mode, it returns an 【230†`io.BufferedRandom`】. When buffering is disabled, the raw stream, a subclass of 【231†`io.RawIOBase`】, 【232†`io.FileIO`】, is returned.
L741: See also the file handling modules, such as 【233†`fileinput`】, 【234†`io`】 (where `open()` is declared), 【235†`os`】, 【236†`os.path`】, 【237†`tempfile`】, and 【238†`shutil`】.
L742: 
L743: Raises an 【91†auditing event】 `open` with arguments `path`, `mode`, `flags`.
L744: 
L745: The `mode` and `flags` arguments may have been modified or inferred from the original call.
L746: 
L747: Changed in version 3.3:
L748: 
L749:   * The opener parameter was added.
L750: 
L751:   * The `'x'` mode was added.
L752:   * 【239†`IOError`】 used to be raised, it is now an alias of 【209†`OSError`】.
L753: 
L754:   * 【240†`FileExistsError`】 is now raised if the file opened in exclusive creation mode (`'x'`) already exists.
L755: 
L756: Changed in version 3.4:
L757: 
L758:   * The file is now non-inheritable.
L759: 
L760: Changed in version 3.5:
L761:   * If the system call is interrupted and the signal handler does not raise an exception, the function now retries the system call instead of raising an 【241†`InterruptedError`】 exception (see 【242†PEP 475†peps.python.org】 for the rationale).
L762: 
L763:   * The `'namereplace'` error handler was added.
L764: 
L765: Changed in version 3.6:
L766: 
L767:   * Support added to accept objects implementing 【243†`os.PathLike`】.
L768: 
L769:   * On Windows, opening a console buffer may return a subclass of 【231†`io.RawIOBase`】 other than 【232†`io.FileIO`】.
L770: Changed in version 3.11: The `'U'` mode has been removed.
L771: 
L772: Changed in version 3.15: UTF-8 is now the default encoding, instead of the platform-dependent locale encoding (【244†PEP 686†peps.python.org】).

L774: ord(character, / (Positional-only parameter separator (PEP 570)))【52†¶】
L775: 
L776: 
L777: Return the ordinal value of a character.
L778: If the argument is a one-character string, return the Unicode code point of that character. For example, `ord('a')` returns the integer `97` and `ord('€')` (Euro sign) returns `8364`. This is the inverse of 【13†`chr()`】.
L779: 
L780: If the argument is a 【94†`bytes`】 or 【92†`bytearray`】 object of length 1, return its single byte value. For example, `ord(b'a')` returns the integer `97`.
L781: 
L782: pow(base, exp, mod=None)【53†¶】
L783: Return base to the power exp; if mod is present, return base to the power exp, modulo mod (computed more efficiently than `pow(base, exp) % mod`). The two-argument form `pow(base, exp)` is equivalent to using the power operator: `base**exp`.
L784: When arguments are builtin numeric types with mixed operand types, the coercion rules for binary arithmetic operators apply. For 【37†`int`】 operands, the result has the same type as the operands (after coercion) unless the second argument is negative; in that case, all arguments are converted to float and a float result is delivered. For example, `pow(10, 2)` returns `100`, but `pow(10, -2)` returns `0.01`.
L785: For a negative base of type `int` or 【25†`float`】 and a non-integral exponent, a complex result is delivered. For example, `pow(-9, 0.5)` returns a value close to `3j`. Whereas, for a negative base of type `int` or `float` with an integral exponent, a float result is delivered. For example, `pow(-9, 2.0)` returns `81.0`.
L786: For 【37†`int`】 operands base and exp, if mod is present, mod must also be of integer type and mod must be nonzero. If mod is present and exp is negative, base must be relatively prime to mod. In that case, `pow(inv_base, -exp, mod)` is returned, where inv_base is an inverse to base modulo mod.
L787: 
L788: Here’s an example of computing an inverse for `38` modulo `97`:
L789: 
L790:     >>> pow(38, -1, mod=97)
L791:     23
L792:     >>> 23 * 38 % 97 == 1
L793:     True
L794: Changed in version 3.8: For 【37†`int`】 operands, the three-argument form of `pow` now allows the second argument to be negative, permitting computation of modular inverses.
L795: 
L796: Changed in version 3.8: Allow keyword arguments. Formerly, only positional arguments were supported.
L797: 
L798: print(*objects, sep=' ', end='\n', file=None, flush=False)【54†¶】
L799: 
L800: 
L801: Print objects to the text stream file, separated by sep and followed by end. sep, end, file, and flush, if present, must be given as keyword arguments.
L802: All non-keyword arguments are converted to strings like 【151†`str()`】 does and written to the stream, separated by sep and followed by end. Both sep and end must be strings; they can also be `None`, which means to use the default values. If no objects are given, `print()` will just write end.
L803: The file argument must be an object with a `write(string)` method; if it is not present or `None`, 【245†`sys.stdout`】 will be used. Since printed arguments are converted to text strings, `print()` cannot be used with binary mode file objects. For these, use `file.write(...)` instead.
L804: 
L805: Output buffering is usually determined by file. However, if flush is true, the stream is forcibly flushed.
L806: 
L807: Changed in version 3.3: Added the flush keyword argument.
L808: class property(fget=None, fset=None, fdel=None, doc=None)【55†¶】
L809: 
L810: 
L811: Return a property attribute.
L812: 
L813: fget is a function for getting an attribute value. fset is a function for setting an attribute value. fdel is a function for deleting an attribute value. And doc creates a docstring for the attribute.
L814: A typical use is to define a managed attribute `x`:
L815: 
L816:     class C:
L817:         def __init__(self):
L818:             self._x = None
L819: 
L820:         def getx(self):
L821:             return self._x
L822: 
L823:         def setx(self, value):
L824:             self._x = value
L825: 
L826:         def delx(self):
L827:             del self._x
L828: 
L829:         x = property(getx, setx, delx, "I'm the 'x' property.")
L830: 
L831: 
L832: If c is an instance of C, `c.x` will invoke the getter, `c.x = value` will invoke the setter, and `del c.x` the deleter.
L833: If given, doc will be the docstring of the property attribute. Otherwise, the property will copy fget’s docstring (if it exists). This makes it possible to create read-only properties easily using 【55†`@property`】 as a 【106†decorator】:
L834: 
L835:     class Parrot:
L836:         def __init__(self):
L837:             self._voltage = 100000
L838: 
L839:         @property
L840:         def voltage(self):
L841:             """Get the current voltage."""
L842:             return self._voltage
L843: The `@property` decorator turns the `voltage()` method into a “getter” for a read-only attribute with the same name, and it sets the docstring for voltage to “Get the current voltage.”
L844: 
L845: @getter【246†¶】
L846: 
L847: 
L848: @setter【247†¶】
L849: 
L850: 
L851: @deleter【248†¶】
L852: A property object has `getter`, `setter`, and `deleter` methods usable as decorators that create a copy of the property with the corresponding accessor function set to the decorated function. This is best explained with an example:
L853: 
L854:     class C:
L855:         def __init__(self):
L856:             self._x = None
L857: 
L858:         @property
L859:         def x(self):
L860:             """I'm the 'x' property."""
L861:             return self._x
L862: 
L863:         @x.setter
L864:         def x(self, value):
L865:             self._x = value
L866:         @x.deleter
L867:         def x(self):
L868:             del self._x
L869: This code is exactly equivalent to the first example. Be sure to give the additional functions the same name as the original property (`x` in this case.)
L870: 
L871: The returned property object also has the attributes `fget`, `fset`, and `fdel` corresponding to the constructor arguments.
L872: 
L873: Changed in version 3.5: The docstrings of property objects are now writeable.
L874:

L887: repr(object, / (Positional-only parameter separator (PEP 570)))【57†¶】
L888: Return a string containing a printable representation of an object. For many types, this function makes an attempt to return a string that would yield an object with the same value when passed to 【22†`eval()`】; otherwise, the representation is a string enclosed in angle brackets that contains the name of the type of the object together with additional information often including the name and address of the object.
L889: A class can control what this function returns for its instances by defining a 【251†`__repr__()`】 method.
L890: This class has a custom representation that can be evaluated:
L891: 
L892:     class Person:
L893:        def __init__(self, name, age):
L894:           self.name = name
L895:           self.age = age
L896: 
L897:        def __repr__(self):
L898:           return f"Person({self.name!r}, {self.age!r})"

L901: reversed(object, / (Positional-only parameter separator (PEP 570)))【58†¶】
L902: Return a reverse 【149†iterator】. The argument must be an object which has a 【252†`__reversed__()`】 method or supports the sequence protocol (the 【253†`__len__()`】 method and the 【195†`__getitem__()`】 method with integer arguments starting at `0`).

L904: round(number, ndigits=None)【59†¶】
L905: 
L906: 
L907: Return number rounded to ndigits precision after the decimal point. If ndigits is omitted or is `None`, it returns the nearest integer to its input.
L908: For the built-in types supporting `round()`, values are rounded to the closest multiple of 10 to the power minus ndigits; if two multiples are equally close, rounding is done toward the even choice (so, for example, both `round(0.5)` and `round(-0.5)` are `0`, and `round(1.5)` is `2`). Any integer value is valid for ndigits (positive, zero, or negative). The return value is an integer if ndigits is omitted or `None`. Otherwise, the return value has the same type as number.
L909: For a general Python object `number`, `round` delegates to `number.__round__`.
L910: 
L911: Note
L912: 
L913: The behavior of `round()` for floats can be surprising: for example, `round(2.675, 2)` gives `2.67` instead of the expected `2.68`. This is not a bug: it’s a result of the fact that most decimal fractions can’t be represented exactly as a float. See 【254†Floating-Point Arithmetic: Issues and Limitations】 for more information.

L920: setattr(object, name, value, / (Positional-only parameter separator (PEP 570)))【61†¶】
L921: This is the counterpart of 【29†`getattr()`】. The arguments are an object, a string, and an arbitrary value. The string may name an existing attribute or a new attribute. The function assigns the value to the attribute, provided the object allows it. For example, `setattr(x, 'foobar', 123)` is equivalent to `x.foobar = 123`.
L922: name need not be a Python identifier as defined in 【255†Names (identifiers and keywords)】 unless the object chooses to enforce that, for example in a custom 【147†`__getattribute__()`】 or via `__slots__`. An attribute whose name is not an identifier will not be accessible using the dot notation, but is accessible through 【29†`getattr()`】 etc..
L923: 
L924: Note
L925: Since 【178†private name mangling】 happens at compilation time, one must manually mangle a private attribute’s (attributes with two leading underscores) name in order to set it with `setattr()`.

L927: class sentinel(name, / (Positional-only parameter separator (PEP 570)), * (Keyword-only parameters separator (PEP 3102)), repr=None)【62†¶】
L928: Return a new unique sentinel object. name must be a 【151†`str`】, and is used by default as the returned object’s representation:
L929: 
L930:     >>> MISSING = sentinel("MISSING")
L931:     >>> MISSING
L932:     MISSING
L933: 
L934: 
L935: The optional repr argument can be used to specify a different representation:
L936: 
L937:     >>> MISSING = sentinel("MISSING", repr="<MISSING>")
L938:     >>> MISSING
L939:     <MISSING>
L940: 
L941: 
L942: Sentinel objects are true and compare equal only to themselves. They are intended to be compared with the `is` operator.
L943: `sentinel` does not support subclassing.
L944: 
L945: Shallow and deep copies of a sentinel object return the object itself.
L946: 
L947: Sentinels are conventionally assigned to a variable with a matching name. Sentinels defined in this way can be used in type hints:
L948: 
L949:     MISSING = sentinel("MISSING")
L950: 
L951:     def next_value(default: int | MISSING = MISSING):
L952:         ...
L953: 
L954: 
L955: Sentinel objects support the | operator for use in type expressions.
L956: `Pickling` is supported for sentinel objects that are placed in the global scope of a module under a name matching the sentinel’s name, and for sentinels placed in class scopes with a name matching the qualified name of the sentinel. Other sentinels, such as those defined in a function scope, are not picklable. The identity of the sentinel is preserved after pickling:
L957: 
L958:     import pickle
L959: 
L960:     PICKLABLE = sentinel("PICKLABLE")
L961:     assert pickle.loads(pickle.dumps(PICKLABLE)) is PICKLABLE
L962: 
L963:     class Cls:
L964:         PICKLABLE = sentinel("Cls.PICKLABLE")
L965: 
L966:     assert pickle.loads(pickle.dumps(Cls.PICKLABLE)) is Cls.PICKLABLE
